tech-da-excel.title: Excel & Sheets for analysts
tech-da-excel.description: Excel and Google Sheets from zero to advanced: formulas, lookups, pivots, what-if analysis and dashboards - practised with small realistic tables.

courses.title: Excel foundations: cells, formulas and references
courses.summary: Build confident spreadsheet habits: clean tables, core formulas, relative/absolute references, and conditional aggregation on realistic sales data.
outcomes: Write formulas using operators, ranges and functions
Choose relative, absolute or mixed references correctly
Summarise data with SUMIF(S), COUNTIF(S) and AVERAGEIF
Use IF, IFS, AND, OR to classify rows
Structure a worksheet so others can audit it

lessons.title: Lab: Your first formulas and ranges

scenes.text: Asha joins a retail chain as a junior analyst. Her manager sends a sheet of daily store sales and says: 'Tell me the week's total and the best day.'
She realises she must stop typing numbers on a calculator and let the sheet calculate.

steps.title: Formulas start with =
steps.body:
Every formula begins with **=**. Excel evaluates operators in the order brackets, powers, multiplication/division, then addition/subtraction. `=2+3*4` gives 14, not 20.

A **range** like `B2:B8` means every cell from B2 to B8. Functions take ranges: `=SUM(B2:B8)`, `=AVERAGE(B2:B8)`, `=MAX(B2:B8)`, `=MIN(B2:B8)`, `=COUNT(B2:B8)` (counts numbers only).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Sales in B2:B8 are 120, 95, 143, 110, 160, 210, 180.

- Total: `=SUM(B2:B8)` = 1018
- Average: `=AVERAGE(B2:B8)` = 145.43 (rounded)
- Best day: `=MAX(B2:B8)` = 210
- Days recorded: `=COUNT(B2:B8)` = 7

steps.title: Common mistake: numbers stored as text
steps.body: If a number is left-aligned with a green triangle it may be **text**. SUM ignores it silently and your total is too low. Fix with Data > Text to Columns, `VALUE()`, or multiply by 1.

activity.prompt: Daily sales are in B2:B8. Complete the formulas.
activity.text: Total sales: =___(B2:B8). Highest day: =___(B2:B8). Number of days with data: =___(B2:B8).

quiz.why: Multiplication is done before addition: 3*4=12, plus 2 = 14.

quiz.q: Which function counts only cells that contain numbers?
quiz.why: COUNT counts numeric cells; COUNTA counts any non-empty cell.

quiz.q: A SUM total is smaller than expected and some values are left-aligned. Likely cause?
options: Some numbers are stored as text
Excel is in manual mode only

quiz.q: What does the range A1:C2 contain?

lessons.title: Lab: Relative, absolute and mixed references

scenes.text: Asha must add 18% GST to 200 product prices. Her manager typed the rate once in cell F1.
She copies the formula down and the results turn to zero after row 2 - the rate cell moved!

steps.title: Why references shift
steps.body:
When you copy `=B2*F1` down one row it becomes `=B3*F2`: both parts are **relative**. To lock the rate, write `=B2*$F$1`. The `$` freezes the column and/or row.

- `A1` relative (moves both ways)
- `$A$1` absolute (never moves)
- `A$1` row locked, column moves
- `$A1` column locked, row moves

Press **F4** while editing to cycle through these.

steps.title: Mixed reference in a table
steps.body:
A multiplication grid: row headers 1-5 in A2:A6, column headers 1-5 in B1:F1. In B2 enter `=$A2*B$1` and fill right and down. Column A and row 1 stay locked while the other part moves.

B2 = 1, C3 = 2 x 2 = 4, F6 = 5 x 5 = 25.

steps.title: Name your assumptions
steps.body: Put the tax rate in its own labelled cell (or a named range `GST_Rate`) instead of burying 0.18 inside formulas. Hard-coded numbers are the top cause of spreadsheet audit failures.

activity.prompt: Price is in B2 and the GST rate is in F1. Make the formula copy-safe.

quiz.q: What does copying =B2*F1 from row 2 to row 3 produce?
quiz.why: Both references are relative so both shift by one row.

quiz.q: Which reference keeps the column fixed but lets the row change?
quiz.why: The $ before the column letter locks the column only.

quiz.q: Which key cycles reference types while editing a formula in Excel for Windows?
Why use a named input cell for a tax rate?
options: So the assumption is visible and changed in one place
quiz.why: Single, labelled assumptions make models auditable.

lessons.title: Lab: Conditional totals: SUMIF, COUNTIF, AVERAGEIF

scenes.text: The regional head asks: 'How much did the North region sell, and how many orders were above 150?'
Asha knows filtering by hand will not scale to 20,000 rows.

steps.title: Conditional aggregation
steps.body:
`=SUMIF(range, criteria, sum_range)` adds values where a condition holds.
`=COUNTIF(range, criteria)` counts matches. `=AVERAGEIF(range, criteria, avg_range)` averages them.

For several conditions use the **S** versions: `=SUMIFS(sum_range, range1, crit1, range2, crit2)` - note sum_range comes FIRST. Criteria with operators are text: `">150"`, `"<>North"`, or concatenated `">"&F1`.

steps.title: Common mistake: mismatched range sizes
steps.body: In SUMIFS every criteria range must be the same size as the sum range, otherwise you get #VALUE!. Also trailing spaces in data ('North ') break matches - clean with TRIM first.

activity.prompt: Region (A2:A7): North, South, North, East, North, South. Amount (B2:B7): 120, 200, 90, 310, 160, 75. What does =SUMIFS(B2:B7,A2:A7,"North",B2:B7,">100") return?

quiz.why: SUMIFS puts sum_range first, unlike SUMIF.

quiz.q: How do you count values greater than the number in F1?
quiz.why: The operator is text concatenated with the cell value.

quiz.q: 'North ' with a trailing space will not match "North". Best fix?
quiz.why: TRIM removes extra spaces so matches work.

quiz.q: COUNTIF(A2:A7,"South") on the sample region list returns?

lessons.title: Lab: Logic: IF, IFS, AND, OR

scenes.text: Sales reps earn 2% commission under 100 units, 3% from 100 to 199, and 5% from 200 up.
Asha must calculate it for 60 reps without eyeballing each row.

steps.title: Decisions in formulas
steps.body:
`=IF(test, value_if_true, value_if_false)`. Combine tests with `AND()` / `OR()`. For many tiers use `IFS(test1,val1,test2,val2,...,TRUE,default)` or nest IFs from highest to lowest.

Example tier formula for units in B2: `=IFS(B2>=200,0.05,B2>=100,0.03,TRUE,0.02)`. Order matters - Excel stops at the first TRUE.

steps.title: Wrap risky lookups
steps.body: `=IFERROR(formula, "n/a")` hides errors, but use it deliberately: hiding #DIV/0! can also hide real data problems. Prefer testing the cause, e.g. `=IF(C2=0,"",B2/C2)`.

activity.prompt: Commission is 2% under 100 units, 3% for 100-199, 5% for 200+. A rep sold 199 units at 40 revenue per unit. What commission (currency) is earned?

quiz.q: In IFS, what happens if conditions are listed lowest-tier first (>=0 first)?
options: The first test is always true so later tiers never run
quiz.why: IFS stops at the first TRUE.

quiz.q: Which function returns TRUE only if both conditions hold?
A rep sold exactly 100 units under the tier rule (3% from 100). Which test places them correctly?

scenes.text: Asha's team shares one workbook for monthly expenses; last month it was a mess of typed totals.
She decides to rebuild it so another analyst can audit it in five minutes.

steps.title: Design rules of a good workbook
steps.body:
- One table per sheet, headers in row 1, no merged cells inside data
- Inputs (rates, thresholds) in a labelled Assumptions area
- Calculations by formula, never pasted values
- Totals use whole-column or table references so new rows are included
- Check cells: e.g. `=SUM(detail)-total` should equal 0

steps.title: A check cell
steps.body: Detail amounts sum to 48,250 but the summary says 48,520. A check cell `=SUM(B2:B40)-E2` returns -270, instantly exposing a transposed-digit typing error (48,250 vs 48,520).

steps.title: Freeze, format, protect
steps.body: Freeze the header row (View > Freeze Panes), format as an Excel Table (Ctrl+T) for auto-expanding ranges, and lock formula cells before sharing.

activity.prompt: Put the workbook-building steps in a sensible order.

Clean text, trim spaces and fix number formats
Put rates and thresholds in an Assumptions area
Add formulas using absolute references to assumptions
Add check cells that should equal zero
Freeze headers and protect formula cells before sharing

courses.title: Lookups, text and date functions
courses.summary: Join tables with XLOOKUP/VLOOKUP/INDEX-MATCH, clean messy text, and do date arithmetic the way analysts do on real extracts.
outcomes: Use XLOOKUP and VLOOKUP with exact match
Build INDEX-MATCH for left lookups and two-way lookups
Clean text with TRIM, LEFT, MID, TEXTJOIN, SUBSTITUTE
Compute ages, tenures and month buckets from dates
Diagnose #N/A and #REF! errors

scenes.text: Orders list only a product code. Prices live on another sheet.
Asha needs the price next to each order without copy-pasting 5,000 times.

steps.title: Lookup basics
steps.body:
`=VLOOKUP(key, table, col_index, FALSE)` searches the FIRST column of `table` and returns the value from column number `col_index`. The last argument FALSE (or 0) means exact match - **always** use it for codes.

`=XLOOKUP(key, lookup_array, return_array, "not found")` is the modern replacement: it looks in any column, defaults to exact match, and returns a default for misses.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Price table A2:B5: P10 -> 250, P20 -> 400, P30 -> 125, P40 -> 90.

- `=VLOOKUP("P30",A2:B5,2,FALSE)` = 125
- `=XLOOKUP("P50",A2:A5,B2:B5,"missing")` = missing

An order of 4 units of P20 is worth 4 x 400 = 1,600.

steps.title: The approximate-match trap
steps.body: VLOOKUP's default last argument is TRUE (approximate, needs sorted data). On unsorted codes it silently returns wrong rows. Always type FALSE.

activity.prompt: Price table is in A2:B5 (code, price). Return the price for the code in D2 with exact match.

quiz.q: What does the final FALSE in VLOOKUP mean?
Which function can return values from a column LEFT of the lookup column without helpers?
quiz.why: XLOOKUP uses separate lookup and return arrays.
The 4th argument is the not-found result.

quiz.q: 4 units of a product priced 400 are ordered. Order value?

scenes.text: A freight rate depends on both the weight band and the zone - a grid, not a list.
Asha needs a lookup that matches on a row AND a column.

steps.title: INDEX + MATCH
steps.body:
`=MATCH(value, range, 0)` returns the POSITION of value. `=INDEX(range, n)` returns the nth item. Together: `=INDEX(B2:B10, MATCH(F1, A2:A10, 0))`.

Two-way: `=INDEX(grid, MATCH(row_key, row_headers, 0), MATCH(col_key, col_headers, 0))`.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Grid rows (weight band) A2:A4 = 1kg, 5kg, 10kg; column headers B1:D1 = ZoneA, ZoneB, ZoneC. Values: 1kg 40,55,70; 5kg 60,80,110; 10kg 95,130,180.

Rate for 5kg to ZoneC: MATCH("5kg") = 2, MATCH("ZoneC") = 3, so INDEX(B2:D4,2,3) = 110.

steps.title: Why analysts still learn INDEX-MATCH
steps.body: It works in every Excel/Sheets version, survives inserted columns (unlike a hard-coded col_index), and is the base of dynamic reporting.

activity.prompt: Rate grid (rows 1kg/5kg/10kg, columns ZoneA/ZoneB/ZoneC): 1kg 40,55,70; 5kg 60,80,110; 10kg 95,130,180. What does =INDEX(B2:D4, MATCH("10kg",A2:A4,0), MATCH("ZoneB",B1:D1,0)) return?

quiz.q: Why is INDEX-MATCH safer than VLOOKUP with a hard-coded column number?
quiz.why: Column numbers change when columns are inserted; MATCH finds the header.

quiz.q: The third argument of MATCH should be 0 for what behaviour?
INDEX(B2:D4,2,3) in the sample grid returns?

scenes.text: The CRM export has 'RAVI  kumar ', 'priya SHARMA' and emails in one column with phone numbers.
Joins fail because the same customer is spelled five ways.

steps.title: Text toolkit
steps.body:
- `TRIM(t)` removes extra spaces; `CLEAN(t)` removes non-printing characters
- `UPPER`, `LOWER`, `PROPER` change case
- `LEFT(t,n)`, `RIGHT(t,n)`, `MID(t,start,n)` slice; `LEN(t)` counts characters
- `FIND(find,t)` locates text (case-sensitive); `SEARCH` is not
- `SUBSTITUTE(t,old,new)` replaces; `TEXTJOIN(sep,TRUE,range)` joins

steps.title: Chain cleaning
steps.body: `=PROPER(TRIM(A2))` turns '  RAVI  kumar ' into 'Ravi Kumar'. Always clean BEFORE you join or pivot.

activity.prompt: Cell A2 contains EMP-00417-IN. Complete the formula to extract the five-digit number as text.

quiz.why: TRIM leaves single inner spaces; PROPER capitalises words.

quiz.q: Which function is case-insensitive when locating text?
quiz.why: FIND is case-sensitive; SEARCH is not.

quiz.q: Why clean text before a lookup?
options: Hidden spaces and case differences cause misses

scenes.text: HR wants each employee's tenure in years and the join-month for a hiring chart.
Asha finds dates stored as 'dd-mm-yyyy' text from a Linux export.

steps.title: How Excel stores dates
steps.body:
A date is a **serial number** (days since 1 Jan 1900 in the default system). Times are fractions of a day. Subtracting dates gives days: `=B2-A2`.

- `TODAY()`, `YEAR`, `MONTH`, `DAY`, `WEEKDAY`
- `EOMONTH(date, n)` end of month n months away
- `DATEDIF(start,end,"Y"/"M"/"D")` whole years/months/days
- `NETWORKDAYS(start,end)` working days
- `TEXT(date,"mmm-yyyy")` formats as a label

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Start 15-Mar-2021, end 10-Nov-2024.

- `=DATEDIF(start,end,"Y")` = 3 whole years
- `=DATEDIF(start,end,"M")` = 43 whole months
- `=EOMONTH(start,0)` = 31-Mar-2021
- `=TEXT(start,"mmm-yyyy")` = Mar-2021

steps.title: dd-mm vs mm-dd
steps.body: 05/06/2024 is 5 June in India/UK and 6 May in the US. Importing text dates with the wrong locale silently swaps day and month for dates up to the 12th. Check with a date after the 12th.

activity.prompt: An employee joined on 15-Mar-2021. Today is 10-Nov-2024. How many COMPLETE months of tenure (DATEDIF with "M")?

quiz.q: Subtracting two dates in Excel gives?
quiz.why: Dates are serial numbers; difference = days.

quiz.q: Which function returns working days between two dates?
Why can imported text dates be dangerous?
options: Day and month may be swapped by locale
quiz.why: Ambiguous formats are parsed by locale.

scenes.text: Operations sends orders.csv: product codes with spaces, text dates, no prices.

steps.title: The routine
steps.body: 1. Trim/clean key columns. 2. Convert dates to real dates. 3. Look up price with exact match and a 'missing' default. 4. Compute value = qty x price. 5. Count lookup misses - they are data-quality findings, not noise.

steps.title: Why count misses
steps.body: 5,000 orders, 37 return 'missing' because codes were retired. Reporting that 0.74% of lines had no price is a finding; silently returning 0 would understate revenue.

steps.title: Keep raw data untouched
steps.body: Never edit the raw sheet. Build a clean sheet by formulas so the process is repeatable next week.

courses.title: Pivot tables, cleaning and validation
courses.summary: Summarise thousands of rows in seconds with PivotTables, clean imported data, and protect your sheets with validation and conditional formatting.
outcomes: Place fields in Rows, Columns, Values and Filters
Show values as % of total and group dates
Clean duplicates, text-numbers and blanks
Apply data validation and conditional formatting
Verify pivot results against source data

scenes.text: Leela must answer 'sales by region and quarter' from 5,000 order rows by noon.
A PivotTable does what 40 SUMIFS would.

steps.title: The four areas
steps.body: Insert > PivotTable on a clean Excel Table. **Rows** and **Columns** hold categories, **Values** hold numbers to aggregate (Sum, Count, Average, Max, Distinct Count via the data model), **Filters/Slicers** restrict the data. A pivot reads a **snapshot**: after changing the source press **Refresh** (Alt+F5). Source needs: one header row, no blanks in header, no merged cells, one record per row.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Region in Rows, Quarter in Columns, Sum of Amount in Values gives a region x quarter grid with grand totals. Double-click any cell to see the underlying rows (drill-down).

steps.title: Stale pivots
steps.body: A pivot does not update automatically. Wrong numbers in a report are often just an un-refreshed pivot.

activity.prompt: Where does each field belong in the pivot?

quiz.q: PivotTables update when source data changes?

options: One header row and no merged cells

lessons.title: Lab: Show Values As, grouping and calculated fields

scenes.text: The CEO wants each region's share of total and sales by month, not by day.
Leela uses Show Values As and Group.

steps.title: Beyond Sum
steps.body: Show Values As: % of Grand Total, % of Column/Row Total, % of Parent, Running Total, Difference From, Rank. **Group** dates by Month/Quarter/Year (right-click a date). Group numbers into bins (e.g. order value bands of 500). A **calculated field** computes on summed fields (e.g. Price = Amount/Qty uses sums, then divides), a common trap for averages.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Regions: North 370, South 275, East 310, West 245 (total 1,200). North's % of grand total = 370/1200 = 30.8%.

scenes.text: Leela's CRM export has duplicate rows, text-numbers and blank cells.
Order matters when cleaning.

steps.title: Cleaning toolkit
steps.body:
- Remove Duplicates (Data tab) - decide the key columns first
- Text to Columns, `VALUE`, Paste Special > Multiply by 1 for text-numbers
- `TRIM`, `CLEAN`, Find & Replace for stray characters
- Go To Special > Blanks to fill or flag blanks
- Flash Fill (Ctrl+E) for pattern extraction
- **Power Query** (Data > Get & Transform): repeatable, recorded steps that refresh with new files

Always work on a copy; record row counts before/after.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: 5,200 rows, 120 exact duplicates removed -> 5,080 rows. Document it: 'removed 120 exact duplicates (2.3%)'.

steps.title: Prevention and highlighting
steps.body: **Data Validation** (Data tab): drop-down lists from a range, whole-number limits, date ranges, custom formulas (e.g. `=COUNTIF($A:$A,A2)=1` for unique IDs); add input and error messages. **Conditional formatting**: highlight cells rules, top/bottom, data bars, colour scales, icon sets, or formula rules like `=$D2<TODAY()` to flag overdue rows (use mixed references so the rule applies to the whole row).

courses.title: What-if analysis, finance and forecasting functions
courses.summary: Goal Seek, scenarios, data tables, loan and investment functions (PMT, NPV, IRR), growth rates and simple forecasting.
outcomes: Use Goal Seek and scenario thinking
Compute loan payments with PMT
Evaluate projects with NPV and IRR

scenes.text: Profit must reach 2,00,000; Leela changes the price until it does.
Goal Seek automates the guessing.

steps.title: What-if tools
steps.body: **Goal Seek** (Data > What-If Analysis): set a formula cell to a target value by changing ONE input cell. **Scenario Manager** stores named sets of inputs (Best/Base/Worst). **Data Tables** recalculate a formula for a range of input values (one- or two-variable sensitivity). **Solver** (add-in) handles several inputs and constraints. steps.title: Discounting
steps.body: **NPV** = sum of cash flows discounted at the required rate. Excel's `=NPV(rate, values)` assumes the FIRST value is one period from now - so the initial outlay (time 0) is added separately: `=NPV(10%, 400, 400, 400) - 1000`. **IRR** is the rate that makes NPV zero: `=IRR(range)` with the outlay included as a negative first value. Accept projects with NPV > 0 (IRR above the required return). IRR can mislead with multiple sign changes or mutually exclusive projects of different sizes.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: NPV = 400/1.1 + 400/1.21 + 400/1.331 - 1000 = -5.26. IRR = 9.70% (slightly under 10%), so the project is marginally unattractive.

steps.title: Growth and trend

Forecast only a short distance beyond the data and show the uncertainty.

outcomes: Solve nth-highest problems with DENSE_RANK or OFFSET
Find and explain duplicates

scenes.text: The interviewer asks: 'Find the second highest distinct salary.'
Think out loud: ties, NULLs, fewer than 2 rows.

steps.title: Approaches
steps.body: 1) `SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees)`. 2) `DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC)` then `rank = 2`. 3) `SELECT DISTINCT salary ... ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1`. Mention edge cases: ties (DISTINCT / DENSE_RANK, not ROW_NUMBER), fewer than two distinct values (should return NULL, not an error), NULL salaries. Narrate the trade-offs: the window method generalises to nth.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Salaries: 150, 120, 120, 90, 110, 110, 70, 65, 100. Distinct sorted desc: 150, 120, 110, 100, 90, 70, 65. Second highest distinct = 120.

steps.title: RANK vs DENSE_RANK
steps.body: RANK leaves gaps after ties, so 'rank 2' may not exist when two people share rank 1. DENSE_RANK avoids it.

activity.prompt:
Return the 2nd highest DISTINCT salary as the column second_highest.

Tables: employees(emp_id, name, dept, salary, manager_id) and logins(user_id, login_date). Salaries are in thousands.
activity.solution: WITH r AS (SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rk FROM employees) SELECT MAX(salary) AS second_highest FROM r WHERE rk = 2;
activity.hint: MAX(salary) WHERE rk = 2 returns NULL when it does not exist.

options: NULL instead of no row when the rank does not exist

scenes.text: 'For each user, what is the longest streak of consecutive login days?'
The famous islands trick.

steps.title: The trick
steps.body: Consecutive dates minus an increasing row number are constant within a streak. Compute `julianday(login_date) - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date)` as `grp`; group by user and grp, count rows for streak length, then take the MAX per user. Deduplicate dates first if a user can log in twice a day. Explain why it works: each day increases both the date and the row number by 1.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: User 3: 2, 3, 4, 5 May -> streak 4. User 1: 1-3 May -> 3. User 2: 1 May and 3 May are not consecutive -> longest streak 1.

Tables: employees(emp_id, name, dept, salary, manager_id) and logins(user_id, login_date). Salaries are in thousands.
activity.solution: WITH g AS (SELECT user_id, login_date, julianday(login_date) - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date) AS grp FROM (SELECT DISTINCT user_id, login_date FROM logins)), s AS (SELECT user_id, grp, COUNT(*) AS len FROM g GROUP BY user_id, grp) SELECT user_id, MAX(len) AS max_streak FROM s GROUP BY user_id ORDER BY user_id;
activity.hint: Group by user_id, grp then MAX the counts per user.

scenes.text: 'What is the probability two dice sum to 7?' and 'A family has two children, at least one is a boy. P(both boys)?'

steps.title: Method
steps.body: List equally likely outcomes. Two dice: 36 outcomes; sum 7 occurs for (1,6),(2,5),(3,4),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1) = 6, so P = 6/36 = 1/6. Two children (order matters): BB, BG, GB, GG; at least one boy removes GG, leaving 3; both boys is 1 of 3, so P = 1/3. State assumptions (fair dice, boy/girl equally likely and independent). Check with a quick sanity argument.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: P(at least one six in two dice) = 1 - (5/6)^2 = 11/36 = 0.3056.

steps.title: Model explanations
steps.body: **p-value**: 'If there were really no effect, how often would we see a result this extreme by luck? A small p says luck is an unlikely explanation.' **Confidence interval**: 'A range of plausible values for the true number; wider means less certainty.' **Correlation vs causation**: 'Two things moving together does not mean one causes the other; ice cream sales and drownings both rise with hot weather.' Use a concrete business example for each and avoid jargon.

story.title: How many users do we need?

scenes.text: 'Baseline conversion is 10%. You want to detect a 1 percentage point lift. How many users per group?'
Use a rule of thumb, then refine.

steps.title: Rule of thumb
steps.body: For 80% power and 5% two-sided significance, the sample per group is about n = 16 x p(1-p) / d^2, where d is the absolute difference to detect. With p = 0.10 and d = 0.01: n = 16 x 0.09 / 0.0001 = 14,400 per group. Halving d quadruples n. Duration = n x 2 / daily eligible traffic, rounded up to full weeks. Mention guardrails and randomisation units (user, not session).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: If 4,000 eligible users arrive per day and each group needs 14,400 users: total 28,800 / 4,000 = 7.2 days, so run 2 full weeks.

steps.body: `int`, `float`, `str`, `bool`, `None`. Variables are labels, not boxes: `revenue = 1200`. Use `type(x)` to check. **f-strings** embed values: `f"Revenue: {revenue:,}"` gives `Revenue: 1,200`; format specs: `:,` thousands, `:.2f` two decimals, `:.1%` percent (0.256 -> 25.6%), `:>8` right-align.

lessons.title: Lab: Numbers: floats, rounding and money

scenes.text: A reconciliation script shows a one-paisa difference.

steps.title: Float facts
steps.body: Binary floats store approximations: `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004`. Compare with a tolerance (`abs(a-b) < 1e-9` or `math.isclose`). `round(x, 2)` uses **banker's rounding** (round half to even) on the binary value, so `round(2.675, 2)` gives 2.67 and `round(0.5)` gives 0. For money use integers (paise) or `decimal.Decimal`.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: `from decimal import Decimal; Decimal('0.1') + Decimal('0.2')` is exactly `Decimal('0.3')`.

steps.title: Report rounding last
steps.body: Round only for display. Rounding each line before summing can differ from summing then rounding.

steps.title: Lists
steps.body: Lists are ordered, mutable: `append`, `extend`, `pop`, `sorted(x)` (new list) vs `x.sort()` (in place), `sum`, `min`, `max`, `len`. **Comprehension**: `[expr for x in items if cond]`. Copy a list with `x[:]` or `list(x)` - assignment `y = x` only adds a second label.

steps.title: Aliasing
steps.body: `b = a; b.append(1)` also changes `a`. Use `b = a.copy()` when you need an independent list.

steps.title: Dicts
steps.body: `d = {key: value}`; `d[k]`, `d.get(k, default)`, `d[k] = v`, `k in d`, `d.items()`. steps.title: datetime
steps.body: `datetime.strptime('2024-01-05', '%Y-%m-%d')` parses; `.date()` drops time; `.strftime('%Y-%m')` formats; subtracting dates gives a `timedelta` with `.days`. Format codes: %Y year, %m month, %d day, %b month name, %A weekday. ISO strings (YYYY-MM-DD) sort chronologically as text. Always state the expected format; ambiguous 05/06/2024 formats must be agreed with the data owner.

scenes.text: Ishaan has the same GST calculation in six scripts.

steps.title: Functions
steps.body: `def name(args): ... return value`. Use default arguments (`rate=0.18`), keyword arguments at call sites for clarity, and a one-line docstring. Functions should do one thing, have no hidden global dependencies, and return values rather than print (printing is for the caller). Avoid mutable default arguments (`def f(x, acc=[])` shares one list across calls).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: `def with_gst(amount, rate=0.18): return round(amount * (1 + rate), 2)`; `with_gst(1000)` -> 1180.0; `with_gst(1000, rate=0.05)` -> 1050.0.

steps.title: Mutable default trap
steps.body: Use `acc=None` then `if acc is None: acc = []`.

steps.title: Defensive code
steps.body: `try/except SpecificError` handles expected failures; never use a bare `except:`. `raise ValueError('message')` signals bad input. `assert condition, 'message'` documents and checks invariants (e.g. totals reconcile). `finally` always runs. Log what you skipped. Fail loudly for impossible states; recover quietly only for expected, counted ones.

scenes.text: Ishaan has 7 order amounts and wants maths without loops.
numpy applies operations to whole arrays.

steps.title: numpy basics
steps.body: `np.array([...])` creates a typed array. Arithmetic is element-wise (**vectorised**): `a * 1.18`. Aggregates: `a.sum()`, `a.mean()`, `a.max()`, `a.std(ddof=1)` (sample SD; the default ddof=0 is the population SD). Boolean masks filter: `a[a > 1000]`. `np.where(cond, x, y)` is a vector IF. Convert numpy scalars with `int()`/`float()` before printing for clean output.

steps.title: ddof
steps.body: numpy's std() defaults to the POPULATION formula; pandas' .std() defaults to the SAMPLE formula. Always check.

courses.summary: Learn to ask a database business questions: select and filter rows, sort, handle NULLs, aggregate with GROUP BY and HAVING, and compute with CASE - all in runnable SQLite labs.
outcomes: Write SELECT queries with WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT and DISTINCT
Reason correctly about NULL and three-valued logic
Aggregate with COUNT, SUM, AVG and GROUP BY/HAVING
Create categories with CASE and format dates/text
Read the logical order of a SQL query

lessons.title: Lab: SELECT, WHERE and ORDER BY

scenes.text: On day one the sales manager asks Kabir: 'Show me all delivered orders above 1,000, biggest first.'
Kabir opens the orders table and writes his first real query.

steps.title: Anatomy of a query
steps.body:
`SELECT columns FROM table WHERE condition ORDER BY column [DESC] LIMIT n;`

WHERE filters rows using `=`, `<>`, `<`, `>`, `BETWEEN`, `IN (...)`, `LIKE 'A%'`, combined with `AND`, `OR`, `NOT`. Text values use single quotes. ORDER BY sorts ascending by default; add DESC for largest first.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
`SELECT order_id, amount FROM orders WHERE status = 'delivered' AND amount > 1000 ORDER BY amount DESC;`

On the shop data this returns orders 103 (5000), 105 (3500), 108 (2200), 101 (1200).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- `WHERE status = delivered` (missing quotes) looks for a column named delivered
- `AND` binds tighter than `OR`: use brackets when mixing
- Without ORDER BY the row order is NOT guaranteed

activity.prompt:
List order_id and amount of delivered orders above 1000, biggest amount first.

Tables: customers(customer_id, name, city, segment, signup_date), orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, amount), products(product_id, name, category, price), order_items(order_id, product_id, qty).
activity.starter:
SELECT order_id, amount
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'delivered'
-- add the amount filter and ORDER BY
;
activity.solution: SELECT order_id, amount FROM orders WHERE status = 'delivered' AND amount > 1000 ORDER BY amount DESC;
activity.hint: Combine two conditions with AND, then ORDER BY amount DESC.

quiz.q: Which clause filters rows before grouping?
quiz.why: WHERE filters individual rows; HAVING filters groups.

quiz.q: What is the default sort order of ORDER BY?
In WHERE a = 1 OR b = 2 AND c = 3, which part is evaluated first?
quiz.why: AND has higher precedence than OR.

quiz.q: Which pattern matches names starting with 'A'?

scenes.text: Kabir needs the list of cities customers live in, and the three most recent signups.
He also finds customers with missing data and must decide how to treat it.

steps.title: Removing duplicates, trimming output
steps.body:
`SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers;` returns each city once. `LIMIT 3` returns the first three rows - pair it with ORDER BY or you get arbitrary rows.

**NULL** means unknown. `NULL = NULL` is not true; use `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL`. `COALESCE(x, 0)` replaces NULL with a default. Aggregates like AVG ignore NULLs, but COUNT(*) counts rows.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
`SELECT name, signup_date FROM customers ORDER BY signup_date DESC LIMIT 3;` returns Farhan (2023-05-11), Esha (2023-04-02), Divya (2023-03-18).

`SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers ORDER BY city;` returns Chennai, Delhi, Mumbai, Pune.

steps.title: NULL traps
steps.body: `WHERE city <> 'Delhi'` silently drops rows where city is NULL. `NOT IN (subquery)` returns nothing if the subquery contains a NULL. Always decide how NULLs should behave.

activity.prompt:
Return the distinct cities of customers in alphabetical order.

Tables: customers(customer_id, name, city, segment, signup_date), orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, amount), products(product_id, name, category, price), order_items(order_id, product_id, qty).
activity.solution: SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers ORDER BY city;
activity.hint: DISTINCT goes right after SELECT.

quiz.q: How do you test for a missing value?

quiz.why: COALESCE returns the first non-NULL argument.

quiz.q: Does AVG(x) include NULL rows in the denominator?

lessons.title: Lab: Aggregates, GROUP BY and HAVING

scenes.text: The CFO wants revenue and order counts by status, and only statuses with more than one order.
Kabir learns that every non-aggregated column must appear in GROUP BY.

steps.title: Grouping
steps.body:
`COUNT(*)`, `SUM(x)`, `AVG(x)`, `MIN(x)`, `MAX(x)` collapse many rows to one. `GROUP BY col` makes one row per distinct value. `HAVING` filters groups after aggregation; WHERE filters rows before.

Logical order: FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> ORDER BY -> LIMIT. That is why you cannot use a SELECT alias in WHERE.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
`SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM orders GROUP BY status HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;`

Only 'delivered' has more than one order: 7 orders totalling 14,050.

steps.title: COUNT(DISTINCT x)
steps.body: Use `COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)` to count unique customers, not orders. Mixing the two up is the classic KPI bug.

activity.prompt:
For each status, show status, number of orders (n) and total amount (revenue); keep only statuses with more than one order. Order by status.

Tables: customers(customer_id, name, city, segment, signup_date), orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, amount), products(product_id, name, category, price), order_items(order_id, product_id, qty).
activity.starter:
SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
-- group and filter groups
;
activity.solution: SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM orders GROUP BY status HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 ORDER BY status;
activity.hint: GROUP BY status, then HAVING COUNT(*) > 1.

quiz.q: Why can't you use a SELECT alias in WHERE?
quiz.why: Logical order puts WHERE before SELECT.

quiz.q: How many unique customers placed orders?
Which comes first in logical processing?
quiz.why: FROM defines the rows; SELECT is late.

lessons.title: Lab: CASE, dates and text functions

scenes.text: Marketing wants orders labelled Small, Medium or Large, plus a monthly total.
Dates are stored as text in ISO format, which SQLite handles well.

steps.title: CASE and functions
steps.body:
`CASE WHEN cond THEN val ... ELSE val END` creates categories. In SQLite: `strftime('%Y-%m', order_date)` gives the month, `substr`, `upper`, `length`, `round(x,2)` and `||` for concatenation work as expected. Dialects differ: MySQL uses `DATE_FORMAT`, PostgreSQL `date_trunc` / `to_char`, SQL Server `FORMAT`/`EOMONTH`.

Store dates as ISO `YYYY-MM-DD` so text order equals date order.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
`SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month, SUM(amount) FROM orders GROUP BY month;`

Jan = 1200+5000 = 6200; Feb = 800+700 = 1500; Mar = 3500+450+1500+2200+900 = 8550.

steps.title: Pivot with CASE
steps.body: `SUM(CASE WHEN status='delivered' THEN amount ELSE 0 END)` computes a conditional total - the SQL way to build a pivot table column.

activity.prompt:
Label each order: 'Large' if amount >= 2000, 'Medium' if amount >= 1000, else 'Small'. Show order_id and size, ordered by order_id.

Tables: customers(customer_id, name, city, segment, signup_date), orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, amount), products(product_id, name, category, price), order_items(order_id, product_id, qty).
activity.starter:
SELECT order_id,
  CASE
    -- add WHEN branches
  END AS size
FROM orders
ORDER BY order_id;
activity.solution: SELECT order_id, CASE WHEN amount >= 2000 THEN 'Large' WHEN amount >= 1000 THEN 'Medium' ELSE 'Small' END AS size FROM orders ORDER BY order_id;
activity.hint: List the biggest threshold first; CASE stops at the first match.

quiz.q: In CASE, if two WHEN conditions are true, which result is returned?
Why store dates as YYYY-MM-DD text in SQLite?
options: Text sort order equals chronological order

quiz.q: Which expression gives a conditional total?
options: SUM(CASE WHEN status='delivered' THEN amount ELSE 0 END)
quiz.why: CASE inside an aggregate is the standard pivot idiom.

quiz.q: March total of the sample orders (3500+450+1500+2200+900) is?

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone: Weekly sales summary query

scenes.text: Kabir must produce the Monday summary: per city, how many delivered orders and how much revenue.
The orders table has no city - that lives in customers. He needs a join, a filter and grouping together.

steps.title: Plan before typing
steps.body: Write the business question in plain words, list the tables and the join key, decide the grain (one row per what?), then add filters and aggregates. Grain = one row per city.

steps.title: Join key
steps.body: orders.customer_id matches customers.customer_id. `FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id` gives every order with its customer's city.

steps.title: Test with a small check
steps.body: Verify by hand on 2-3 rows. Delivered orders: Mumbai has 101,102,109 = 2900; Delhi has 103,105,108 = 10700; Pune has 106 = 450.

activity.prompt:
For delivered orders only, show city, number of orders (orders) and total revenue, highest revenue first.

Tables: customers(customer_id, name, city, segment, signup_date), orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, amount), products(product_id, name, category, price), order_items(order_id, product_id, qty).
activity.starter:
SELECT c.city, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(o.amount) AS revenue
FROM orders o
-- join customers, filter delivered, group by city
;
activity.solution: SELECT c.city, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(o.amount) AS revenue FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE o.status = 'delivered' GROUP BY c.city ORDER BY revenue DESC;
activity.hint: JOIN customers on customer_id, WHERE status, GROUP BY city.

Delivered revenue for Delhi in the sample is?
Which is the join key between orders and customers?
What should you do before trusting a query on 10 million rows?

courses.title: Joins: combining tables correctly
courses.summary: Master INNER, LEFT, multi-table joins, anti-joins, self-joins and UNION - and learn to spot the join mistakes that inflate revenue numbers.
outcomes: Choose INNER vs LEFT joins for a business question
Find missing relationships with anti-joins
Chain 3+ tables without double counting
Use self-joins and UNION/UNION ALL
Debug row-count explosions

scenes.text: Order rows only hold customer ids; managers want names.
Kabir joins the two tables on the shared key.

steps.title: How INNER JOIN works
steps.body: `FROM a JOIN b ON a.key = b.key` keeps only rows with a match in BOTH tables. Use short aliases (`o`, `c`) and qualify columns (`o.amount`). If a key is not unique in `b`, rows of `a` are repeated - the root of most double-counting bugs.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
`SELECT c.name, o.order_id FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.order_id;`

Returns 9 rows because every order has a valid customer. Farhan (no orders) does not appear.

steps.title: Forgetting the ON clause
steps.body: Without a join condition you get a cross join: 9 orders x 6 customers = 54 rows. Always check row counts after a join.

activity.prompt:
List order_id, customer name and amount for all orders over 2000, ordered by order_id.

Tables: customers(customer_id, name, city, segment, signup_date), orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, amount), products(product_id, name, category, price), order_items(order_id, product_id, qty).
activity.starter:
SELECT o.order_id, c.name, o.amount
FROM orders o
-- JOIN customers here
WHERE o.amount > 2000
ORDER BY o.order_id;
activity.solution: SELECT o.order_id, c.name, o.amount FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE o.amount > 2000 ORDER BY o.order_id;
activity.hint: JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id.

options: Only rows matching in both tables
All rows of the left table

quiz.q: A join without ON between 9 and 6 rows yields?
A non-unique key in the joined table causes?
options: Duplicated rows on the other side

scenes.text: Retention wants to email customers who signed up but never bought.
An inner join cannot show absence - a LEFT JOIN can.

steps.title: Keeping unmatched rows
steps.body: `LEFT JOIN` keeps ALL rows of the left table; right-side columns are NULL where no match exists. An **anti-join** finds missing relationships: `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.key IS NULL`. Alternative: `WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 ...)`.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: `SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.order_id IS NULL;` returns Farhan, the only customer without orders.

steps.title: Filter in ON, not WHERE
steps.body: A condition on the right table in WHERE (`o.status='delivered'`) turns a LEFT JOIN back into an INNER JOIN, because NULL rows are removed. Put such filters in the ON clause.

activity.prompt:
Show every customer's name and their number of delivered orders (0 if none), ordered by name.

Tables: customers(customer_id, name, city, segment, signup_date), orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, amount), products(product_id, name, category, price), order_items(order_id, product_id, qty).
activity.starter:
SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.order_id) AS delivered_orders
FROM customers c
-- LEFT JOIN with the status filter in ON
GROUP BY c.name
ORDER BY c.name;
activity.solution: SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.order_id) AS delivered_orders FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'delivered' GROUP BY c.name ORDER BY c.name;
activity.hint: Put AND o.status = 'delivered' inside the ON clause; COUNT(o.order_id) ignores NULLs.

tests.expect:
Aarav,2
Bina,2
Chirag,1
Divya,1
Esha,1
Farhan,0

options: Rows with no match in the other table

quiz.q: Where should a filter on the right table go to keep a LEFT JOIN a LEFT JOIN?
quiz.why: WHERE would discard the NULL rows.

quiz.q: COUNT(o.order_id) vs COUNT(*) after a LEFT JOIN: which gives 0 for customers with no orders?
quiz.why: COUNT(*) counts the NULL-extended row as 1.

quiz.q: Which customer has no orders in the sample data?
quiz.why: Only customer 6 never appears in orders.

lessons.title: Lab: Joining three or more tables

scenes.text: The merchandise team asks revenue by product category.
That needs order_items and products - and a careful eye on the grain.

steps.title: Multi-table joins
steps.body:
Chain joins one at a time and keep track of the grain. order_items is at **line** level (one row per order x product). Revenue per line = qty x price. Aggregating order-level `amount` after joining to lines would repeat it per line - **fan-out**.

Rule: aggregate at the grain that matches the measure, or pre-aggregate in a subquery/CTE before joining.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
`SELECT p.category, SUM(i.qty * p.price) AS revenue FROM order_items i JOIN products p ON p.product_id = i.product_id GROUP BY p.category ORDER BY p.category;`

Home = Kettle 2x1200 + Lamp 3x800 = 4800; Electronics = Headphones 2x3000 + Mouse 3x500 = 7500; Stationery = Notebook 12x150 = 1800.

steps.title: Fan-out
steps.body: If you sum orders.amount after joining to order_items, an order with 3 lines is counted 3 times. Always compare SUM before and after a join to your trusted total.

activity.prompt:
Revenue per product category using qty x price from order_items and products. Show category and revenue, ordered by category.

Tables: customers(customer_id, name, city, segment, signup_date), orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, amount), products(product_id, name, category, price), order_items(order_id, product_id, qty).
activity.starter:
SELECT p.category, SUM(i.qty * p.price) AS revenue
FROM order_items i
-- join products
GROUP BY p.category
ORDER BY p.category;
activity.solution: SELECT p.category, SUM(i.qty * p.price) AS revenue FROM order_items i JOIN products p ON p.product_id = i.product_id GROUP BY p.category ORDER BY p.category;
activity.hint: JOIN products p ON p.product_id = i.product_id.

options: A join repeating a measure across many rows
quiz.why: One-to-many joins duplicate the one-side values.

quiz.q: A good defence against fan-out is?
options: Compare totals before and after the join

quiz.q: Revenue of a line with qty 3 and price 800 is?

lessons.title: Lab: Self-joins, UNION and set logic

scenes.text: The community team wants pairs of customers living in the same city.
Kabir also needs to stack two result sets into one list.

steps.title: More patterns
steps.body:
A **self-join** joins a table to itself with two aliases: `FROM customers a JOIN customers b ON a.city = b.city AND a.customer_id < b.customer_id` (the `<` removes mirror pairs and self-pairs).

`UNION` stacks result sets and removes duplicates; `UNION ALL` keeps them and is faster. `INTERSECT` and `EXCEPT` do set intersection/difference. Columns must match in number and type.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Pairs in the same city: (Aarav, Chirag) in Mumbai and (Bina, Esha) in Delhi. 2 pairs.

`SELECT city FROM customers UNION SELECT 'Online'` returns the 4 cities plus Online.

steps.title: Prefer UNION ALL
steps.body: Use UNION ALL unless you truly need deduplication - UNION sorts to remove duplicates and can hide data issues.

activity.prompt:
List pairs of customers living in the same city as (a_name, b_name, city), once per pair, ordered by city.

Tables: customers(customer_id, name, city, segment, signup_date), orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, amount), products(product_id, name, category, price), order_items(order_id, product_id, qty).
activity.starter:
SELECT a.name AS a_name, b.name AS b_name, a.city
FROM customers a
-- self-join on city, avoid mirror pairs
ORDER BY a.city;
activity.solution: SELECT a.name AS a_name, b.name AS b_name, a.city FROM customers a JOIN customers b ON a.city = b.city AND a.customer_id < b.customer_id ORDER BY a.city;
activity.hint: Join customers b on same city and a.customer_id < b.customer_id.

options: UNION removes duplicates, UNION ALL keeps them

quiz.q: Why add a.customer_id < b.customer_id in a self-join?
options: To avoid self-pairs and mirror duplicates

quiz.q: Which operator returns rows in the first set but not the second?
UNION requires the queries to have?

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone: Find the customers worth a call

scenes.text: The retention lead wants customers with no delivered order in the data and a list of Corporate customers by lifetime delivered revenue.
Kabir combines LEFT join, aggregation and sorting.

steps.title: Lifetime value with zero
steps.body: Use LEFT JOIN with the status filter in ON, `COALESCE(SUM(...), 0)` so customers with no orders show 0 rather than NULL.

steps.title: Expected shape
steps.body: One row per customer: name, segment, delivered_revenue. Farhan = 0; Bina = 8500; Esha = 2200.

steps.title: Reconcile
steps.body: Add the column totals: the sum of delivered_revenue across customers must equal the sum of delivered amounts in orders (14,050).

activity.prompt:
For each Corporate customer show name and delivered_revenue (0 if none), highest first.

Tables: customers(customer_id, name, city, segment, signup_date), orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, amount), products(product_id, name, category, price), order_items(order_id, product_id, qty).
activity.starter:
SELECT c.name, COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0) AS delivered_revenue
FROM customers c
-- LEFT JOIN delivered orders
WHERE c.segment = 'Corporate'
GROUP BY c.name
ORDER BY delivered_revenue DESC;
activity.solution: SELECT c.name, COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0) AS delivered_revenue FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'delivered' WHERE c.segment = 'Corporate' GROUP BY c.name ORDER BY delivered_revenue DESC;
activity.hint: LEFT JOIN orders o ON ... AND o.status='delivered'.

Sum of customer totals equals sum of the base table

courses.title: Subqueries and CTEs
courses.summary: Break hard questions into readable steps: scalar and correlated subqueries, EXISTS, CTEs, derived tables and multi-step analysis.
outcomes: Use scalar subqueries and IN/EXISTS filters
Write readable CTE pipelines
Aggregate twice (distribution of counts)
Compare groups with segment benchmarks
Choose between subquery, CTE and join

lessons.title: Lab: Scalar subqueries: compare to an average

scenes.text: The ops head asks which orders were larger than the average order.
Kabir needs the average first, then a filter - a query inside a query.

steps.title: Subquery in WHERE
steps.body:
A **scalar subquery** returns one value and can be used anywhere a value fits: `WHERE amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders)`. The inner query runs first.

If the inner query could return more than one row, use `IN` instead of `=`.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Nine orders total 16,250, so the average is 1,805.56. Orders above it: 103 (5000), 105 (3500), 108 (2200).

steps.title: Beware of NULL averages
steps.body: AVG ignores NULL amounts. Decide whether NULL should mean 'zero' or 'unknown' before comparing to an average.

activity.prompt:
Show order_id and amount for orders above the average order amount, ordered by order_id.

Tables: customers(customer_id, name, city, segment, signup_date), orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, amount), products(product_id, name, category, price), order_items(order_id, product_id, qty).
activity.solution: SELECT order_id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders) ORDER BY order_id;
activity.hint: Subquery: SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders.

quiz.q: Average of 16,250 over 9 orders is about?
If a subquery may return many rows you should use?
In execution terms, the inner query of an uncorrelated subquery runs?
options: Once, independently of the outer rows
quiz.why: Uncorrelated subqueries do not reference the outer query.

lessons.title: Lab: IN, EXISTS and correlated subqueries

scenes.text: Quality control wants customers who have at least one returned order.
Kabir tries IN, then learns when EXISTS is clearer.

steps.title: Membership tests
steps.body:
`WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE status='returned')` tests membership. `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status='returned')` is a **correlated** subquery referencing the outer row - it stops at the first match.

`NOT EXISTS` is the NULL-safe way to write an anti-join. `NOT IN` breaks if the subquery returns any NULL.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Only order 107 is returned, belonging to customer 1. The query returns Aarav.

steps.title: Rule of thumb
steps.body: Use EXISTS for 'has at least one', JOIN when you need columns from the other table, and NOT EXISTS for 'has none'.

activity.prompt:
List names of customers who have NO delivered order, ordered by name (use NOT EXISTS).

Tables: customers(customer_id, name, city, segment, signup_date), orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, amount), products(product_id, name, category, price), order_items(order_id, product_id, qty).
activity.solution: SELECT c.name FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'delivered') ORDER BY c.name;
activity.hint: Correlate with o.customer_id = c.customer_id and filter delivered.

options: References columns of the outer query
quiz.why: It depends on the outer row.

quiz.q: Why can NOT IN be dangerous?
options: A NULL in the list makes it return no rows
quiz.why: x NOT IN (..., NULL) is never true.

options: The subquery returns at least one row

scenes.text: Management wants customers whose delivered spend beats the average of customers who spent anything.
Nesting three levels is unreadable; Kabir uses WITH.

steps.title: WITH clauses
steps.body:
A **CTE** (common table expression) names an intermediate result: `WITH totals AS (SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS spend FROM orders WHERE status='delivered' GROUP BY customer_id) SELECT ... FROM totals ...`. Chain several CTEs separated by commas. CTEs are for readability; they are not automatically faster.

Recursive CTEs generate series and walk hierarchies (e.g. org charts).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Delivered spend per customer: Aarav 2000, Bina 8500, Chirag 900, Divya 450, Esha 2200. Average = 14,050/5 = 2,810. Only Bina is above.

steps.title: Name steps like a story
steps.body: Use names such as `orders_clean`, `customer_totals`, `ranked` - each CTE should do ONE thing and be testable on its own by selecting from it.

activity.prompt:
Using a CTE of delivered spend per customer, return the customer_id and spend of customers above the average spend of those customers. Order by customer_id.

lessons.title: Lab: Aggregate twice: distribution of counts

scenes.text: Growth wants: how many customers placed 0, 1, 2, 3 orders?
This needs a count per customer, then a count of customers per count.

steps.title: Two-level aggregation
steps.body: First compute orders per customer (LEFT JOIN so zero-order customers stay), then GROUP BY that number. This 'histogram of counts' is a core analyst move - used for purchase frequency, tickets per user, logins per week.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Orders per customer: 3, 2, 2, 1, 1, 0 -> distribution: 0 orders: 1 customer; 1: 2; 2: 2; 3: 1.

steps.title: Don't lose the zeros
steps.body: Using an inner join drops customers with no orders and your 'zero' bucket disappears - misleading when sizing win-back campaigns.

activity.prompt:
Show n_orders and how many customers have that many orders (customers), ordered by n_orders. Include customers with zero orders.

Tables: customers(customer_id, name, city, segment, signup_date), orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, amount), products(product_id, name, category, price), order_items(order_id, product_id, qty).
activity.starter:
WITH per_customer AS (
  SELECT c.customer_id, COUNT(o.order_id) AS n_orders
  FROM customers c
  LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
  GROUP BY c.customer_id
)
SELECT
;
activity.solution: WITH per_customer AS (SELECT c.customer_id, COUNT(o.order_id) AS n_orders FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id) SELECT n_orders, COUNT(*) AS customers FROM per_customer GROUP BY n_orders ORDER BY n_orders;
activity.hint: SELECT n_orders, COUNT(*) FROM per_customer GROUP BY n_orders.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone: Who beats their segment?

scenes.text: Corporate and Retail customers behave differently; comparing everyone to one average is unfair.

steps.title: Benchmark by group
steps.body: Step 1: customer-level delivered spend (include zeros). Step 2: segment average via GROUP BY. Step 3: join back and compare. Chained CTEs keep each step testable.

steps.title: Expected logic
steps.body: Retail: Aarav 2000, Chirag 900, Divya 450, Farhan 0 -> avg 837.5. Corporate: Bina 8500, Esha 2200 -> avg 5350.

steps.title: Sanity-check
steps.body: A group average multiplied by the group size must equal the group total (837.5 x 4 = 3,350 = 2000+900+450+0).

seg AS (

courses.title: Window functions
courses.summary: Rank, run totals, compare to previous rows and compute moving averages without collapsing rows - the SQL feature that separates juniors from seniors.
outcomes: Rank with ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK
Pick top-N per group
Compute running totals and shares of total
Use LAG/LEAD for period-over-period analysis
Define frames for moving averages

scenes.text: CRM needs each customer's most recent order.
GROUP BY would lose the order details - Kabir needs a window.

steps.title: OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...)
steps.body:
A window function computes over a set of related rows but **keeps every row**. `PARTITION BY` splits into groups; `ORDER BY` orders within each.

- `ROW_NUMBER()` unique 1,2,3 (ties broken arbitrarily)
- `RANK()` ties share a rank and leave gaps (1,1,3)
- `DENSE_RANK()` ties share a rank, no gaps (1,1,2)

To filter on a window result, wrap it in a CTE/subquery - you cannot use it in WHERE directly.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Latest order per customer: rank by order_date DESC within customer_id and keep rn = 1. Customer 1 -> 107 (2024-03-21), 2 -> 105, 3 -> 109, 4 -> 106, 5 -> 108.

steps.title: Ties
steps.body: If two orders share a date, ROW_NUMBER picks one arbitrarily. Add a tiebreaker (order_id) to make results reproducible.

activity.prompt:
Return each customer's latest order: customer_id, order_id, order_date, ordered by customer_id.

Tables: customers(customer_id, name, city, segment, signup_date), orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, amount), products(product_id, name, category, price), order_items(order_id, product_id, qty).
activity.solution: WITH ranked AS (SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC) AS rn FROM orders) SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1 ORDER BY customer_id;
activity.hint: PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC.

quiz.why: They add a column per row.
RANK leaves a gap after ties.

quiz.q: Why wrap a window function in a CTE to filter on it?
options: Window functions need CTEs to run
Window results can't be used in WHERE directly

lessons.title: Lab: Running totals and share of total

scenes.text: Finance asks for cumulative delivered revenue by date and each order's share of the total.
Kabir uses SUM(...) OVER.

steps.title: Aggregates as windows
steps.body:
`SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY d)` gives a running total (default frame: from the first row to the current row, including ties on d). `SUM(x) OVER ()` gives the grand total on every row, so `x * 1.0 / SUM(x) OVER ()` is the share of total.

Partition for per-group totals: `SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id)`.

steps.title: Use ROUND for shares
steps.body: `ROUND(100.0 * amount / SUM(amount) OVER (), 1)` gives a percentage with one decimal; the 100.0 forces decimal arithmetic.

activity.prompt:
For delivered orders, show order_id, order_date, amount and running_total (cumulative amount ordered by order_date, order_id). Order by order_date.

Tables: customers(customer_id, name, city, segment, signup_date), orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, amount), products(product_id, name, category, price), order_items(order_id, product_id, qty).
activity.starter:
SELECT order_id, order_date, amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (
    -- order for the running total
  ) AS running_total
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'delivered'
ORDER BY order_date, order_id;
activity.solution: SELECT order_id, order_date, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date, order_id) AS running_total FROM orders WHERE status = 'delivered' ORDER BY order_date, order_id;
activity.hint: SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date, order_id)

options: The grand total on every row
quiz.why: Empty OVER means the whole set.

quiz.q: To compute per-customer totals on each row use?
Why use 100.0 instead of 100 in a share calculation?
quiz.why: Integer / integer truncates in some engines.

quiz.q: The final running total of the delivered orders is?
quiz.why: Sum of the seven delivered amounts.

lessons.title: Lab: LAG and LEAD: compare to the previous row

scenes.text: Retention wants the gap between consecutive orders of each customer.
Kabir peeks at the previous row with LAG.

steps.title: Peeking at neighbours
steps.body:
`LAG(col, n, default) OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...)` returns the value n rows back; `LEAD` looks forward. Combine with date arithmetic: in SQLite `julianday(a) - julianday(b)` gives days; PostgreSQL uses `a - b`, MySQL `DATEDIFF`.

For month-over-month growth: aggregate by month in a CTE, then `LAG(revenue)`.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Customer 1 orders on 01-05, 02-10, 03-21. Gaps: 36 days (Jan 5 to Feb 10) and 40 days (Feb 10 to Mar 21).

steps.title: First rows
steps.body: The first row in each partition has no previous row, so LAG returns NULL (or your default). Filter or handle it.

activity.prompt:
For customer_id 1, show order_id and days_since_prev (days since the customer's previous order; skip the first order). Order by order_date.

Tables: customers(customer_id, name, city, segment, signup_date), orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, amount), products(product_id, name, category, price), order_items(order_id, product_id, qty).
activity.solution: WITH g AS (SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date, julianday(order_date) - julianday(LAG(order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date)) AS days_since_prev FROM orders) SELECT order_id, days_since_prev FROM g WHERE customer_id = 1 AND days_since_prev IS NOT NULL ORDER BY order_id;
activity.hint: LAG(order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date)

options: The value from the previous row in the window order

quiz.q: The first row of each partition gets what from LAG?
Jan 5 to Feb 10, 2024 is how many days?
quiz.why: 26 days left in January after the 5th + 10 = 36.

lessons.title: Lab: Frames, moving averages and NTILE

scenes.text: Daily numbers jump around; leadership wants a 3-row moving average and customers split into value quartiles.
Frames define exactly which rows a window covers.

steps.title: Window frames
steps.body:
`ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` covers the current row and the two before it: a 3-row moving average = `AVG(x) OVER (ORDER BY d ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)`.

`NTILE(4)` splits ordered rows into 4 near-equal buckets (quartiles). `FIRST_VALUE` / `LAST_VALUE` fetch edge rows (LAST_VALUE needs an explicit frame to the end).

ROWS counts physical rows; RANGE groups ties by value.

steps.title: Small windows at the start
steps.body: The first rows have fewer than 3 values. Decide whether to show partial averages or hide them (e.g. only where row number >= 3).

activity.prompt:
For delivered orders ordered by order_date then order_id, show order_id and the 3-row moving average of amount (ma3, rounded to 2 decimals) for rows that have a full 3 rows (row 3 onwards).

Tables: customers(customer_id, name, city, segment, signup_date), orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, amount), products(product_id, name, category, price), order_items(order_id, product_id, qty).
activity.solution: WITH t AS (SELECT order_id, order_date, ROUND(AVG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date, order_id ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS ma3, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY order_date, order_id) AS rn FROM orders WHERE status = 'delivered') SELECT order_id, ma3 FROM t WHERE rn >= 3 ORDER BY rn;
activity.hint: ORDER BY order_date, order_id ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW

quiz.q: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW covers?
options: The current and two previous rows

quiz.why: It splits ordered rows into 4 groups.

scenes.text: Regional heads want the top 2 delivered orders per city, with rank.
Kabir joins, ranks within city and filters in an outer query.

steps.title: Top-N per group pattern
steps.body: 1) JOIN to get city. 2) `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY amount DESC)` in a CTE. 3) `WHERE rn <= 2`. Use RANK instead if ties should all be kept.

steps.title: Expected
steps.body: Delhi: 103 (5000) and 105 (3500). Mumbai: 101 (1200) and 109 (900). Pune: 106 (450). Chennai has no delivered orders.

steps.title: Test the partition

courses.title: SQL analytics patterns for business questions
courses.summary: The patterns analysts use daily: monthly trends and growth, cohorts and repeat rate, funnels, de-duplication and data-quality checks.
outcomes: Compute monthly trends and growth percentages
Build funnel conversion tables
Create first-order cohorts and repeat-purchase rates
De-duplicate and audit data with SQL
Answer a business question end to end

scenes.text: The board pack needs delivered revenue by month with month-over-month growth.
Kabir aggregates then compares with LAG.

steps.title: Trend recipe
steps.body: 1) Bucket dates with `strftime('%Y-%m', d)` (PostgreSQL: `date_trunc('month', d)`). 2) Aggregate. 3) Compare to previous with LAG. Growth % = (this - prev) / prev x 100. Guard against dividing by zero or NULL.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Delivered revenue: Jan 6200, Feb 800, Mar 7050. Feb growth = (800-6200)/6200 = -87.1%; Mar growth = (7050-800)/800 = 781.25%.

steps.title: Partial months
steps.body: A half-finished current month always looks like a crash. Exclude it or label it clearly.

activity.prompt:
Delivered revenue by month: month (YYYY-MM), revenue and growth_pct versus the previous month rounded to 1 decimal (NULL for the first month). Order by month.

Tables: customers(customer_id, name, city, segment, signup_date), orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, amount), products(product_id, name, category, price), order_items(order_id, product_id, qty).
activity.starter:
WITH m AS (
  SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month, SUM(amount) AS revenue
  FROM orders WHERE status = 'delivered'
  GROUP BY month
)
SELECT month, revenue,
  -- growth % using LAG
  AS growth_pct
FROM m ORDER BY month;
activity.solution: WITH m AS (SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM orders WHERE status = 'delivered' GROUP BY month) SELECT month, revenue, ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)) / LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 1) AS growth_pct FROM m ORDER BY month;
activity.hint: 100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)) / LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)

quiz.q: A partial current month should be?
Division by a NULL or zero previous value yields?
options: NULL or an error unless guarded

scenes.text: Growth tracks visit -> cart -> checkout -> paid for 10 visitors this week.
Each step must count distinct users.

steps.title: Funnel table
steps.body:
Count DISTINCT users at each step, then divide by the first step. Order steps explicitly with CASE (alphabetical order is wrong). Report both step-to-step conversion and overall conversion; the biggest absolute drop is the first place to investigate.

Tables: events(user_id, step, ts).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: visit 10, cart 6, checkout 4, paid 3. Overall conversion 30%. Step conversions: cart/visit 60%, checkout/cart 66.7%, paid/checkout 75%.

steps.title: Count users not events
steps.body: A user viewing the cart 5 times is one user. COUNT(*) inflates the funnel; COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) is correct.

activity.prompt: Funnel: for each step show step, users (distinct) and pct_of_visits (rounded to 1 decimal), ordered visit, cart, checkout, paid. Table: events(user_id, step, ts).
activity.starter:
SELECT step, COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS users,
  -- percent of visit users
  AS pct_of_visits
FROM events
GROUP BY step
ORDER BY CASE step WHEN 'visit' THEN 1 WHEN 'cart' THEN 2 WHEN 'checkout' THEN 3 ELSE 4 END;
activity.solution: SELECT step, COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS users, ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) / (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) FROM events WHERE step = 'visit'), 1) AS pct_of_visits FROM events GROUP BY step ORDER BY CASE step WHEN 'visit' THEN 1 WHEN 'cart' THEN 2 WHEN 'checkout' THEN 3 ELSE 4 END;
activity.hint: Divide by a scalar subquery counting distinct visit users.

quiz.q: Overall conversion for 3 paid of 10 visits?
Why order funnel steps with CASE?

scenes.text: The CMO asks what share of customers ordered more than once.
Kabir counts orders per customer and flags repeaters.

steps.title: Cohort thinking
steps.body:
A **cohort** groups customers by a shared start (first order month, signup month). Retention asks: of the cohort, how many do X in month +1, +2...

**Repeat rate** = customers with 2+ orders / customers with 1+ orders. First order date per customer: `MIN(order_date)` grouped by customer.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Customers with orders: 5 (Aarav 3, Bina 2, Chirag 2, Divya 1, Esha 1). Repeaters: 3. Repeat rate = 60%.

steps.title: Define the metric
steps.body: State whether cancelled/returned orders count. Different definitions give different repeat rates - write yours in the report footer.

activity.prompt:
Repeat purchase rate among customers with at least one order: show customers_with_orders, repeaters and repeat_rate_pct (rounded to 1 decimal).

Tables: customers(customer_id, name, city, segment, signup_date), orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, amount), products(product_id, name, category, price), order_items(order_id, product_id, qty).
activity.solution: WITH c AS (SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) SELECT COUNT(*) AS customers_with_orders, SUM(CASE WHEN n >= 2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS repeaters, ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN n >= 2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS repeat_rate_pct FROM c;
activity.hint: Use SUM(CASE WHEN n >= 2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END).

options: A group sharing a common starting event
Customers with 2+ orders / customers with 1+ orders

scenes.text: The customer table has suspicious duplicates and orders with no customer.
Before any dashboard, Kabir audits the data.

steps.title: Audit queries
steps.body:
- Duplicates: `GROUP BY key HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`
- Orphans: LEFT JOIN ... WHERE parent.key IS NULL
- NULL rates: `SUM(col IS NULL)` / `COUNT(*)`
- Range checks: negative amounts, future dates
- Keep one row: `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY updated_at DESC) = 1`

Write checks as queries that should return 0 rows, and re-run them on every refresh.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Every order's customer_id exists in customers, so the orphan check returns 0 rows. Customers with no orders: 1 (Farhan) - fine, not an error.

steps.title: Don't delete in analysis
steps.body: Analysts flag and exclude with transparent filters; they rarely delete source data. Record how many rows were excluded and why.

activity.prompt:
Data-quality check: list order_ids whose customer_id does not exist in customers (orphans). It should return NO rows - so output the count instead as orphan_orders.

Tables: customers(customer_id, name, city, segment, signup_date), orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, amount), products(product_id, name, category, price), order_items(order_id, product_id, qty).
activity.solution: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orphan_orders FROM orders o LEFT JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE c.customer_id IS NULL;
activity.hint: LEFT JOIN customers and test c.customer_id IS NULL.

quiz.q: An orphan record is one whose parent key?
options: Does not exist in the parent table

quiz.q: When deleting suspect rows in analysis, you should?
options: Document counts and reasons, prefer filters

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone: Answer a stakeholder question end to end

scenes.text: A manager emails: 'Which category is driving revenue, and which city buys it most?'
Kabir turns a vague ask into a precise metric, query and short answer.

steps.title: From ask to answer
steps.body: 1) Clarify: revenue = qty x price from order_items of delivered orders only. 2) Grain: category x city. 3) Query. 4) Sanity check totals. 5) Write the answer first, evidence second.

steps.title: Answer shape
steps.body: 'Electronics leads delivered revenue; Delhi is its biggest buyer (...). Evidence: table below. Caveat: 9 orders only.'

steps.title: State caveats
steps.body: Mention the sample size and definition. A confident answer with a stated limitation builds trust.

activity.prompt:
Delivered revenue (qty x price) by category and city: show category, city, revenue, ordered by revenue descending, then category, then city.

Tables: customers(customer_id, name, city, segment, signup_date), orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, amount), products(product_id, name, category, price), order_items(order_id, product_id, qty).
activity.starter:
SELECT p.category, c.city, SUM(i.qty * p.price) AS revenue
FROM orders o
-- join order_items, products, customers
-- keep delivered only, group, order
;

lessons.title: Lab: Centre: mean, median and mode

scenes.text: A warehouse logs 10 days of order counts: 12, 15, 14, 10, 18, 20, 15, 13, 15, 40. The manager asks 'what is a normal day?'
Dev notices one huge day (40) pulls the average up.

steps.title: Three centres
steps.body:
- **Mean** = sum / n. Uses every value; pulled by outliers.
- **Median** = middle value of the sorted data (average of the middle two if n is even). Robust to outliers.
- **Mode** = most frequent value.

For skewed data (incomes, delivery times, order values) report the median, often alongside the mean.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Sum = 172, n = 10, so mean = 17.2. Sorted: 10,12,13,14,15,15,15,18,20,40. Middle two are 15 and 15, median = 15. Mode = 15. The mean (17.2) is higher than the median because of the 40.

steps.title: Mean of means
steps.body: Averaging group averages is wrong unless groups are equal in size. Use a weighted mean: sum(value x weight)/sum(weights).

lessons.title: Lab: Spread: variance, standard deviation, range

steps.title: Measuring spread
steps.body:
- **Range** = max - min (very sensitive to outliers)
- **Variance** = average squared deviation from the mean. Sample variance divides by **n-1** (Bessel's correction) because the sample mean is estimated from the same data.
- **Standard deviation** = square root of variance, in original units.

Population: divide by N (`pstdev`). Sample: divide by n-1 (`stdev`).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: For the 10 daily counts: sum of squared deviations = 649.6. Sample variance = 649.6/9 = 72.18. Sample SD = 8.5 orders. Range = 30.

steps.title: Coefficient of variation
steps.body: CV = SD / mean compares spread across different units or scales (e.g. revenue in lakhs vs. units). A CV of 0.2 means SD is 20% of the mean.

steps.title: Five-number summary
steps.body:
Min, Q1, median, Q3, max. **IQR** = Q3 - Q1. The Tukey rule flags values below Q1 - 1.5xIQR or above Q3 + 1.5xIQR. Different tools compute quartiles slightly differently (Excel QUARTILE.INC vs EXC, pandas, R), so small differences are normal - state your method.

Here we use the median-of-halves method.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Sorted: 10,12,13,14,15 | 15,15,18,20,40. Lower half median Q1 = 13, upper half median Q3 = 18, IQR = 5. Upper fence = 18 + 7.5 = 25.5; lower fence = 13 - 7.5 = 5.5. The 40 is above the fence: flag it.

steps.title: Flag, then investigate
steps.body: An outlier is a prompt to ask why (promotion? bulk order? typo?), not an automatic deletion. Report results with and without it when it matters.

q3 = st.median(upper)

lessons.title: Lab: Weighted averages and Simpson's paradox

scenes.text: Ad A converts better for both phone and desktop users, yet Ad B looks better overall.

steps.title: Aggregation can mislead
steps.body:
**Simpson's paradox**: a trend appears in each group but reverses when groups are combined, because group sizes differ. The overall rate is a **weighted average** of group rates, weighted by group size. Always check whether groups are comparable before reading an aggregate.

Fix: compare within segments, or standardise to the same mix.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Ad A: phone 20/100 (20%), desktop 90/400 (22.5%) -> overall 110/500 = 22.0%.
Ad B: phone 70/400 (17.5%), desktop 10/50 (20%) -> overall 80/450 = 17.8%.
Here A is better everywhere and overall. Now imagine A shows mostly to hard-to-convert phones and B to desktops: the overall ordering can flip even if A wins each segment.

steps.title: Ask about the mix
steps.body: Before reading any overall rate, ask: did both options see the same kind of users? Randomisation protects against this; observational data does not.

steps.title: Core rules
steps.body: P(A) is between 0 and 1. **Complement**: P(not A) = 1 - P(A). **Independent AND**: P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B). **OR**: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B). For 'at least one', compute 1 minus 'none'.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: P(no six in one roll) = 5/6. For 3 independent rolls = (5/6)^3 = 125/216. P(at least one six) = 1 - 125/216 = 91/216 = 0.4213.

lessons.title: Lab: Conditional probability and Bayes' theorem

scenes.text: A screening has 90% sensitivity and a 5% false-positive rate; 1% of people have the condition.
A positive result does NOT mean 90% chance of having it.

steps.title: Updating beliefs
steps.body:
P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B). **Bayes**: P(D|+) = P(+|D) P(D) / P(+), where P(+) = P(+|D)P(D) + P(+|not D)P(not D). The **base rate** P(D) matters hugely when the condition is rare.

Same logic: fraud alerts, spam filters, churn flags.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Out of 10,000 people: 100 have it, 90 test positive; of 9,900 healthy, 5% = 495 test positive. P(D|+) = 90/(90+495) = 0.1538 - about 15.4%.

steps.title: Base-rate neglect
steps.body: Ignoring how rare an event is leads to over-trusting alerts. A fraud model with 5% false positives on 0.1% fraud will mostly flag innocent customers.

scenes.text: Mean satisfaction in a sample of 64 is 52 with SD 8. What can we say about all customers?

steps.title: Sampling distribution
steps.body: The **standard error** (SE) of a sample mean is SD/sqrt(n). It measures how much sample means vary. By the **central limit theorem**, for reasonably large n the distribution of sample means is approximately normal, whatever the population shape. Bigger n shrinks SE slowly: to halve the SE you need four times the data.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: SE = 8/sqrt(64) = 8/8 = 1. With n = 256 the SE would be 8/16 = 0.5.

steps.title: Bias beats size
steps.body: A huge but biased sample (e.g. only people who answered a pop-up) is worse than a small random one. SE only measures random error, not bias.

steps.title: CI = estimate +/- margin
steps.body: Margin = critical value x SE. For 95% with large n use 1.96 (use the t-distribution for small n, e.g. t = 2.262 for 9 degrees of freedom). The CI is about the **method**: if we repeated sampling many times, about 95% of such intervals would contain the true mean. It does not mean 'a 95% chance this interval contains it' for a fixed computed interval, though this is the common casual reading.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Mean 52, SE 1: 95% CI = 52 +/- 1.96 = (50.04, 53.96). If the target is 50 or more we are fairly (not absolutely) confident.

courses.title: Hypothesis testing and A/B experiments
courses.summary: p-values, Type I/II errors, power, z-tests for conversion, t-tests for means, multiple-testing traps and how to run a trustworthy A/B test.
outcomes: State null and alternative hypotheses
